content.description: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold had killed the bacteria on a culture dish. That accident produced the first great antibiotic.

hero.hook: A forgotten dish, a patch of mold, and medicine changes forever.

blocks.text: Before antibiotics, a simple infection could kill. A cut, a case of pneumonia, a battlefield wound: the body often had to fight alone.
In **1928**, the Scottish doctor **Alexander Fleming** stumbled on a substance that could kill bacteria. It would be called **penicillin**. But turning it into a real medicine took years more.
Fleming was studying bacteria in London. Back from vacation, he looked over some old culture dishes. On one of them, a **mold** had grown. All around it, the bacteria were dead.

blocks.caption: Fleming and the key idea: something in the mold stops bacteria

blocks.text: The mold belonged to the genus **Penicillium**. Fleming realized that it produced an antibacterial substance, and he named it penicillin. But he could never purify enough of it to treat patients.
Fleming said later that if he had been tidier, he would have thrown the dish away. A messy lab helped the discovery along.
In the early **1940s**, at Oxford, **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Chain** picked up the work. With their team, they isolated penicillin, concentrated it, and tested it on animals and then on humans.
The Second World War made the job urgent: infected soldiers had to be treated. Penicillin went from a lab curiosity to a strategic asset.

sections.title: Oxford turns the idea into a cure

blocks.caption: New industrial methods had to be invented just to grow the mold

blocks.text: Treating millions of people meant producing enormous quantities. The United States industrialized production during the war. Giant tanks grew the mold much the way a brewery makes beer.
In **1945**, Fleming, Florey and Chain received the Nobel Prize. Medicine entered the age of antibiotics.
Today, too many antibiotics badly used have let some bacteria turn **resistant**: the drugs no longer kill them. Fleming had warned about that risk long before.

Penicillin came out of an accident Fleming noticed in **1928**, then became a medicine thanks to Florey, Chain and the wartime industry. It has saved millions of lives, so long as we do not wear it out.

content.title: The discovery of penicillin

Antibiotic resistance.explanation: An evolutionary phenomenon by which bacteria develop mechanisms to resist antibiotics. Predicted by Fleming as early as 1945, it now kills 1.27 million people per year - one of the main health threats of the 21st century.

Howard Florey.explanation: Australian pharmacologist who, with Ernst Chain, transformed Fleming's observation into a stable and injectable medicine on an industrial scale.

Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain.displayTerm: Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain
Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain.explanation: Oxford researchers who purified penicillin starting in 1939 and tested it on humans in 1941. Without their work, Fleming's discovery would have remained a laboratory curiosity. They shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Fleming.

Radioactive decay.explanation: A spontaneous phenomenon by which an unstable atomic nucleus transforms by emitting particles (alpha, beta) or radiation (gamma). Marie Curie understood that radioactivity was a property of the atom itself, not a chemical reaction.

Staphylococcus.explanation: A genus of bacteria responsible for various infections in humans, some strains of which are now famous for their resistance to treatments.

Syphilis.explanation: A serious sexually transmitted infection, once an incurable plague, which was the first major successful target of penicillin.

antibiotic resistance.explanation: An evolutionary phenomenon by which bacteria develop mechanisms to resist antibiotics. Predicted by Fleming as early as 1945, it now kills 1.27 million people per year - one of the main health threats of the 21st century.

quiz.explanation: When Fleming returned from vacation, he observed that mold had grown on a culture dish and that the bacteria around it had died.
options: A mold had killed the bacteria around it
All the bacteria had survived without any change
The box was completely empty of all life
An unknown fungus made bacteria more resistant
quiz.question: What did Alexander Fleming notice in 1928 on one of his forgotten culture boxes?

quiz.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin by chance in 1928, in London.
quiz.question: When did Alexander Fleming discover penicillin?

quiz.explanation: The mold observed by Fleming belongs to the genus Penicillium, hence the name given to the substance: penicillin.
options: Penicillium
Streptococcus
Escherichia
Aspergillus
quiz.question: What genus does the mold discovered by Fleming belong to?

quiz.explanation: Fleming was unable to purify penicillin sufficiently to treat patients: this work would later fall to Florey and Chain.
options: True
False
quiz.question: True or false: Fleming alone succeeded in purifying penicillin sufficiently to treat the sick.

quiz.explanation: At Oxford, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain isolated, concentrated and tested penicillin, transforming it into a real medicine.
options: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, in Oxford
Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch
Marie Curie and Pierre Curie
James Watson and Francis Crick
quiz.question: Who took up and transformed Fleming's discovery into a real medicine in the early 1940s?

quiz.explanation: The war made it urgent to be able to treat infected soldiers, which pushed penicillin from the laboratory towards a strategic issue.
options: Infected soldiers had to be treated urgently
The civilian laboratories had all closed
Scientists were looking for a chemical weapon
The government wanted to sell it to enemy countries
quiz.question: Why did World War II accelerate the development of penicillin?

quiz.explanation: During the war, the United States industrialized the production of penicillin in giant vats, like for beer.
options: The United States industrialized its production in giant vats during the war
Each hospital grew its own mold separately
It was chemically synthesized without any mold
It was imported in large quantities from Asia
quiz.question: How was penicillin produced in sufficient quantities to treat millions of people?

quiz.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, Florey and Chain developed it in the early 1940s, production became industrialized during the war, then the three researchers received the Nobel Prize in 1945.
items: Fleming observes mold that killed bacteria on a culture dish
Florey and Chain isolate and test penicillin at Oxford
The United States industrialized the production of penicillin during the war
Fleming, Florey and Chain receive Nobel Prize
quiz.question: Put these steps in the history of penicillin in order.

quiz.explanation: Fleming had already warned that bacteria could become resistant to misused antibiotics, a risk that has become very real today.
options: That certain bacteria could become resistant if antibiotics were misused
That penicillin would become toxic over time
That mold could completely disappear
That the price of the drug would become far too high
quiz.question: What risk did Fleming already anticipate regarding antibiotics?
